resources.string: VOZ reads the screen and acts on it only when you give a voice command: open apps, search, tap buttons, scroll, type and read comments. No accounts, no analytics, no servers of its own. Your phone’s speech service turns your voice into text.
Tap the floating mic to give a command.
VOZ lets you control your phone with your voice: open apps, search, tap buttons, scroll, type and hear what’s on the screen. Setup has three steps.
VOZ only listens after you tap the mic, and stops when you tap it again. Your phone’s speech service turns your voice into text.

VOZ needs its accessibility service to read the text on the screen and to tap, scroll and type for you. VOZ reads the screen only when you give a command and does not upload it to a VOZ server. Android speech recognition and other apps may have their own network behavior.

Android will warn that VOZ can take full control of your phone. Every screen reader and voice-control app gets this warning. VOZ only acts on a command you give, and asks before anything that sends, pays, deletes or calls.
1. Open accessibility settings and try to turn on VOZ voice control. Android shows “Restricted setting”. Tap OK.
2. Tap “Open app info” below, then the ⋮ menu in the top corner.
3. Tap “Allow restricted settings” and confirm with your PIN or fingerprint.
4. Come back, tap “Open accessibility settings” and turn on VOZ voice control.
A small mic button floats over other apps, so you can talk to VOZ from anywhere. You can skip this and use Android’s accessibility button instead.
Control your phone with your voice: open apps, search, tap buttons, scroll, type and hear what’s on the screen.
Tap the mic again to stop.
VOZ doesn’t listen while it talks or works. To stop it, tap the mic.
You can also start VOZ with Android’s accessibility button.
Needs two permissions. Turn on to set them up.
The floating mic needs the microphone and “display over other apps” permissions.

Android blocked the microphone for VOZ. Open App info, then Permissions, then Microphone, and choose “Allow only while using the app”.

Test feature for developer and pilot builds. Public versions of VOZ don’t include it.
Add your own Gemini API key first.
Off: VOZ does not send screen data to its experimental cloud feature.
On: only commands VOZ can’t handle on the phone are sent to Google Gemini.
A key is saved on this phone, encrypted.
Use your own paid Gemini API key from aistudio.google.com. It is stored encrypted on this phone and never shown again.
The cloud brain turns off until you add a key again.
Only commands VOZ can’t handle on the phone are sent to Google Gemini, with the text on the screen (up to 150 items). E-mail addresses, IBANs and long numbers are masked first.

Google’s Gemini API terms allow it only for professional use by adults (18 or older), and in the EU, the UK and Switzerland only with a paid key. With a free key, Google may use what is sent to improve its products, and people may read it. Don’t use the cloud brain on banking, health or private chat screens.
VOZ never sends your voice, your contacts or the name of the app in front. You can turn the cloud brain off at any time.
Stored only on this phone: the last 200 entries. Dictated text is kept only as a character count.
Nothing yet. Your commands will appear here.
This deletes every entry on this phone. It can’t be undone.
A cloud reply was not read aloud because it looked unsafe.

VOZ is a voice-control tool for people who find the touch screen hard to use: blind and low-vision users, and people with limited hand movement. You tap the mic or Android’s accessibility button, say a command, and VOZ opens apps, searches, taps buttons, scrolls, types or reads the screen. It asks before anything that sends, pays, deletes or calls.

Your settings, the history (last 200 entries; dictated text only as a character count) and your API key, encrypted with the Android Keystore. Backups are turned off. VOZ has no accounts, no analytics and no servers of its own.

Your phone’s speech service turns your voice into text. VOZ asks for on-device recognition first; if the language pack is missing, the phone’s online service may be used. Replies are spoken by your phone’s text-to-speech engine.

Off by default. When you turn it on, only commands VOZ can’t handle on the phone are sent to Google Gemini, with the text on the screen, personal numbers and e-mail addresses masked. Your voice and the name of the app in front are never sent.
This version has no cloud brain. VOZ does not send screen data to a VOZ server; Android speech recognition and destination apps may have their own network behavior.
Microphone: to hear your command, only after you tap the mic.
Accessibility service: to read the screen and tap, scroll and type when you ask.
Display over other apps: for the floating mic.
Notifications: to show that the floating mic is on, with a button to hide it.
VOZ doesn’t listen while it is talking or working: tap the mic to stop it. It works best when you say the exact name of the button. It has not been tested with every app or phone.
